### Build Refresh Scripts Created at `Project.MM/LocalConfig`

The following manual build refresh automation scripts have been added directly to [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig):

1. **[`refresh_firmware.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/refresh_firmware.bat)**:
   - Double-clickable Windows batch launcher from File Explorer or command prompt.
   - Automatically bypasses PowerShell ExecutionPolicy and keeps the terminal window open with `pause` upon completion so you can review compilation output and binary size.
2. **[`refresh_firmware.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/refresh_firmware.ps1)**:
   - Standalone PowerShell build automation script with 3 sequential stages:
     - **Stage 1 (Asset Sync)**: Runs [`scripts/generate_assets.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/scripts/generate_assets.ps1) to convert HTML/CSS/text files in `data/` into C++ byte arrays in `include/default_assets.h`.
     - **Stage 2 (Virtual SD Mirror)**: Copies `data/www/` directly to `data/network/www/` so Wokwi's virtual SD disk stays updated with your latest web assets.
     - **Stage 3 (Firmware Build)**: Invokes PlatformIO (`pio run` or `python -u -m platformio run`) to recompile the firmware.
     - **Output**: Reports the exact output binary path and size in bytes.
3. **[`build_firmware.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/build_firmware.bat)**:
   - Quick alias launcher directly in `LocalConfig/`.

---

### How to Run

From your terminal inside `Project.MM/LocalConfig`:
```powershell
.\refresh_firmware.bat
# Or:
.\refresh_firmware.ps1
```
Or simply double-click **`refresh_firmware.bat`** (or **`build_firmware.bat`**) in Windows File Explorer. Once complete, click **Stop** then **Start** in VS Code on `diagram.json` to boot the refreshed firmware.

71: ## 1. Executive Pitch & Project Scope
72: 
73: ### 1.1 The 30-Second Elevator Pitch
74: > *"Traditional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web servers rely on power-hungry single-board computers (like Raspberry Pi) or x86 servers drawing 15 to 60 Watts. In this project, we prove that an ultra-low-cost ($4), low-power (<1 Watt) ESP32 dual-core microcontroller can autonomously act as an air-gapped, zero-trust edge NAS and static web host. Interfacing a FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware SPI bus, our firmware delivers full multipart file uploads, chunked downloads, dynamic file deletion, real-time storage telemetry, and static HTML5 website hosting directly to desktop browsers via a local network bridge."*
75: 
76: ### 1.2 Project Scope & Real-World Goals
77: 1. **Air-Gapped Field Data Logging**: In remote industrial sites, environmental sensors can log high-frequency telemetry onto an SD card; field engineers can walk up, connect via local Wi-Fi, and download data or manage logs through an intuitive web UI without any internet connection.
78: 2. **Decentralized Emergency Web Node**: In disaster-relief zones or off-grid scenarios, this node can broadcast emergency static documentation, evacuation maps, and survival guides stored directly on physical flash media.
79: 3. **Ultra-Low Cost & Zero Maintenance**: No spinning hard drives, no noisy fans, zero Linux OS kernel overhead, and instant boot times (< 1 second) with zero vulnerability to common operating system zero-day exploits.
80: 
81: ### 1.3 Core Technical Highlights
82: | Dimension | Specification |
83: | :--- | :--- |
84: | **Microcontroller** | ESP32-WROOM-32 (Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 @ 240 MHz) |
85: | **Volatile RAM** | 520 KB Internal SRAM (320 KB accessible to user heap) |
86: | **Firmware Flash** | 4 MB SPI Flash (Stores compiled code & UI templates via `PROGMEM`) |
87: | **Peripheral Storage** | Virtual MicroSD Block Device formatted with FAT32 |
88: | **Hardware Bus** | VSPI Hardware Peripheral (GPIO 18, 19, 23, 5) |
89: | **Networking** | 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi + HTTP/1.1 REST Web Server |
90: | **Concurrency** | FreeRTOS Multitasking (Core 0 network stack, Core 1 web server & diagnostics) |
91: | **UI Aesthetics** | Glassmorphic Dark UI (`Inter` typography, CSS3 gradients, storage progress bar) |
92:

139: ### 2.2 The Standalone Workspace Philosophy
140: One of the most critical structural decisions made in this repository is **workspace decoupling**:
141: - All installation scripts and dependency managers live in [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup).
142: - The active simulation project [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) is completely self-contained. It contains its own `wokwigw.exe`, `diagram.json`, and `wokwi.toml`.
143: - **Why this matters for your presentation**: If an evaluator asks you to clone the repo or open the project on another laptop, you do **not** have to run everything from the root. You simply open `LocalConfig` in VS Code, start the gateway, press `F1`, and run.
144:

146: 
147: ## 3. Hardware Circuit & Simulation Wiring Nuances
148: 
149: ### 3.1 SPI Hardware Pinout Mapping
150: The ESP32 features two general-purpose SPI hardware peripherals available to user software: **HSPI** (SPI2) and **VSPI** (SPI3). In this project, we interface the MicroSD card module using the default **VSPI** hardware pins:
151: 
152: ```text
153: +-----------------------+                    +-------------------------+
154: |     ESP32 DEVKIT      |                    |   MICROSD CARD MODULE   |
155: |                       |                    |                         |
156: |  [GPIO 5]  (esp:D5)  ----------------------> [CS]   (sd1:CS)         |
157: |  [GPIO 18] (esp:D18) ----------------------> [SCK]  (sd1:SCK)        |
158: |  [GPIO 23] (esp:D23) ----------------------> [MOSI] (sd1:DI)         |
159: |  [GPIO 19] (esp:D19) <---------------------- [MISO] (sd1:DO)         |
160: |  [3V3]     (esp:3V3) ----------------------> [VCC]  (sd1:VCC)        |
161: |  [GND]     (esp:GND.1)---------------------> [GND]  (sd1:GND)        |
162: +-----------------------+                    +-------------------------+
163: ```
164: 
165: | Physical Function | ESP32 GPIO | Diagram Pin Key | MicroSD Module Pin | Protocol Role |
166: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
167: | **Chip Select (CS)** | GPIO 5 | `esp:D5` | `sd1:CS` | Active-low slave select |
168: | **Serial Clock (SCK)** | GPIO 18 | `esp:D18` | `sd1:SCK` | Bus synchronization clock |
169: | **Master Out Slave In** | GPIO 23 | `esp:D23` | `sd1:DI` (Data In) | Commands & data written to SD |
170: | **Master In Slave Out** | GPIO 19 | `esp:D19` | `sd1:DO` (Data Out)| Responses & data read from SD |
171: | **Power Supply** | 3.3V | `esp:3V3` | `sd1:VCC` | Regulated logic power |
172: | **Ground Reference** | 0V | `esp:GND.1` | `sd1:GND` | Common ground |
173: 
174: ---
175: 
176: ### 3.2 Critical Nuance: The Silkscreen `D` Prefix Bug
177: > **Major Talking Point for Evaluators**: Demonstrates deep debugging experience with embedded simulation environments.
178: 
179: In the physical world, engineers refer to GPIO pins by their bare numbers (e.g., GPIO 5). However, inside the Wokwi simulation descriptor [`diagram.json`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/diagram.json), the component `wokwi-esp32-devkit-v1` requires the silkscreen label matching the physical board's printed lettering (`D5`, `D18`, `D19`, `D23`).
180: 
181: - **The Failure**: Declaring `["esp:5", "sd1:CS"]` causes Wokwi to silently fail pin connection because `esp:5` does not match the component pin table. The virtual SPI bus receives no clock or chip-select pulses, resulting in the fatal error:
182:   ```text
183:   [PHASE 1 ERROR] SD Card initialization failed! Check SPI pins.
184:   ```
185: - **The Resolution**: Declaring `["esp:D5", "sd1:CS"]` properly hooks the simulation engine's SPI bus model to the virtual SD card.
186: 
187: ---
188: 
189: ### 3.3 Clock Pin Identifier Nuance (`SCK` vs `CLK`)
190: On standard SPI breakout boards, the clock pin is often labeled `CLK`. In Wokwi's internal part manifest for `wokwi-microsd-card`, the pin is strictly named `SCK`. Using `sd1:CLK` fails schema validation. We corrected this to `sd1:SCK`, ensuring a clean physical layer simulation.
191: 
192: ---
193: 
194: ## 4. Environment Setup & Toolchain Pipeline
195: 
196: ### 4.1 Compilation Pipeline: From C++ to Flash Binary
197: Embedded development differs fundamentally from interpreted languages (Python/JS). Here is how our code transitions from source to execution:
198: 
199: ```mermaid
200: flowchart LR
201:     A[main.cpp] --> C[PlatformIO Compiler / xtensa-esp32-elf-g++]
202:     B[html_templates.h] --> C
203:     D[Arduino Core / SPI / SD / WebServer] --> C
204:     C --> E[Linker: firmware.elf]
205:     E --> F[ESP-IDF esptool.py]
206:     F --> G[firmware.bin 1.24 MB]
207:     G --> H[Wokwi Virtual Flash]
208: ```
209: 
210: 1. **Preprocessing & Inclusion**: `#include "html_templates.h"` in [`main.cpp`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp) injects the HTML layout structures into the translation unit.
211: 2. **Xtensa Cross-Compilation**: `xtensa-esp32-elf-g++` compiles C++ code into machine instructions for the 32-bit Xtensa LX6 architecture.
212: 3. **Firmware Packaging**: PlatformIO invokes `esptool.py` to merge code, bootloader, and partition tables into `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin` (approx. 1.24 MB).
213: 4. **Wokwi Loading**: [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) points directly to this `.bin` file, loading it into virtual SPI flash at address `0x10000`.
214: 
215: ---
216: 
217: ### 4.2 Networking Bridge Architecture (Wokwi Gateway)
218: By default, the Wokwi simulator runs inside an isolated web sandboxed container. The simulated ESP32 connects to an emulated Wi-Fi network (`Wokwi-GUEST`) and is assigned a private IP address (`10.13.37.2`).
219: 
220: Because `10.13.37.2` exists only within the simulator, your host computer's browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) cannot reach it directly. To bridge this gap, we use the **Wokwi IoT Gateway (`wokwigw`)**:

265: ### 5.1 System Execution Flowchart
266: 
267: ```mermaid
268: sequenceDiagram
269:     autonumber
270:     participant Host as Desktop Browser
271:     participant CPU as ESP32 (Core 1)
272:     participant SD as MicroSD Card (VSPI)
273:     participant RTOS as FreeRTOS Diagnostics (Core 0/1)
274: 
275:     Note over CPU, SD: PHASE 1: Storage Boot
276:     CPU->>SD: SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, 5) & SD.begin()
277:     SD-->>CPU: Storage Mounted (FAT32)
278:     CPU->>SD: Check exists("/www/index.html") & exists("/lab_report.txt")
279:     CPU->>SD: Seed default files to SD card
280: 
281:     Note over CPU, Host: PHASE 2: Network & Web Server Boot
282:     CPU->>CPU: WiFi.begin("Wokwi-GUEST") -> Connected (10.13.37.2)
283:     CPU->>CPU: Bind Routes: "/", "/site", "/get", "/upload", "/delete"
284:     CPU->>CPU: server.begin(80)
285:     CPU->>RTOS: Spawn FreeRTOS diagnostic task (runClientTests)
286: 
287:     par Background Diagnostics
288:         RTOS->>CPU: HTTP GET http://127.0.0.1/ -> 200 OK
289:         RTOS->>CPU: HTTP GET http://127.0.0.1/site -> 200 OK
290:         RTOS->>CPU: HTTP GET http://127.0.0.1/get?file=lab_report.txt -> 200 OK
291:     and Interactive User Requests
292:         Host->>CPU: GET http://localhost:9080/
293:         CPU->>SD: Open "/" & iterate directory entries
294:         CPU-->>Host: Stream Glassmorphic Dashboard (HTML + CSS)

300: ### 5.2 Phase 1: Storage Subsystem & Directory Seeding
301: Located in [`main.cpp#L29-L91`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L29-L91):
302: 1. **Explicit VSPI Bus Binding**:
303:    ```cpp
304:    SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, SD_CS_PIN);
305:    SD.begin(SD_CS_PIN, SPI);
306:    ```
307:    Unlike Arduino Uno which only has one SPI bus, the ESP32 has multiple multiplexed buses. Explicitly binding pins prevents pin collision.
308: 2. **Capacity Diagnostics**: Calculates total capacity and used space via `SD.totalBytes()` and `SD.usedBytes()`.
309: 3. **Dynamic Block Device Seeding**:
310:    If the SD card has never been formatted or is blank:
311:    - Creates the directory `/www` via `SD.mkdir("/www")`.
312:    - Writes the static website [`SEED_INDEX_HTML`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h#L264-L387) into `/www/index.html`.
313:    - Creates a default metadata file `/lab_report.txt`.
314: 4. **Directory Traversal**: Recursively scans `/` using `root.openNextFile()` and prints the file tree to the Serial Monitor.
315: 
316: ---
317: 
318: ### 5.3 Phase 2: Network Subsystem, REST Routing & FreeRTOS Telemetry
319: Located in [`main.cpp#L93-L305`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L93-L305):
320: 1. **Virtual Wi-Fi Initialization**: Connects to `Wokwi-GUEST` with non-blocking status polling.
321: 2. **RESTful HTTP Endpoint Table**:
322: 
323: | Method | Endpoint | Handler | Action Performed |
324: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
325: | `GET` | `/` | `handleRoot` | Dynamically builds storage meter, upload form, and file list |
326: | `GET` | `/site` | `handleSite` | Streams `/www/index.html` from SD card with `text/html` MIME |
327: | `GET` | `/get?file=<name>` | `handleDownload` | Streams file binary with `application/octet-stream` header |
328: | `POST`| `/upload` | `handleFileUpload` | Parses incoming multipart stream and writes blocks to SD |
329: | `GET` | `/delete?file=<n>` | `handleDelete` | Deletes file from SD via `SD.remove()` and redirects to `/` |
330: 
331: 3. **Background Diagnostic Task (`runClientTests`)**:
332:    - Uses FreeRTOS `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore` with a 6144-byte stack on Core 1.
333:    - Waits 4 seconds after boot, then executes HTTP client requests against `http://127.0.0.1/` to verify that all endpoints return HTTP `200 OK`.
334:    - Automatically deallocates itself using `vTaskDelete(NULL)`.

338: ## 6. Deep-Dive Engineering Nuances & Design Decisions
339: 
340: ### 6.1 Modular HTML Architecture (`include/html_templates.h`)
341: In novice embedded projects, developers often embed HTML directly inside C++ functions as long, messy string concatenations (`String html = "<html>..."; html += "<body>...";`). This leads to unmaintainable code and rapid heap fragmentation.
342: 
343: We resolved this by isolating the entire presentation layer into [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h):
344: - **C++ Raw String Literals**:
345:   ```cpp
346:   const char NAS_PAGE_HEADER[] PROGMEM = R"rawliteral(
347:   <!DOCTYPE html>
348:   <html>
349:   ...
350:   </html>
351:   )rawliteral";
352:   ```
353:   Using `R"rawliteral(...)rawliteral"` eliminates the need to escape quotes (`\"`) or newlines (`\n`), allowing clean HTML/CSS to be authored exactly as it would appear in a web editor.
354: 
355: ---
356: 
357: ### 6.2 Dispelling the "Single File Flashing" Embedded Myth
358: > **Anticipated Evaluator Question**: *"Since the ESP32 is a microchip, don't we have to write all our code in a single file so it can be flashed?"*
359: 
360: **The Answer**: **No. That is a common misunderstanding of how embedded toolchains operate.**
361: 
362: 1. **Software Engineering Phase (PC Side)**: You can split your code into dozens of `.h` header files and `.cpp` implementation files. This maintains modularity, readability, and separation of concerns.
363: 2. **Compilation & Linking Phase**: The C++ compiler (`xtensa-esp32-elf-g++`) compiles each `.cpp` into an object file (`.o`). The linker then links all object files, libraries (`SD`, `SPI`, `WiFi`), and templates into a single unified binary file: `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin`.
364: 3. **Flashing Phase (Hardware Side)**: The physical flasher (`esptool.py`) writes that single `.bin` file into the ESP32's flash memory.
365: 
366: Therefore, modularizing HTML into `include/html_templates.h` has **zero** runtime penalty and represents industry-standard embedded software engineering.
367: 
368: ---
369: 
370: ### 6.3 Flash Memory Management via `PROGMEM` and `FPSTR`
371: The ESP32 has **4 MB of external SPI Flash ROM**, but only **320 KB of usable internal SRAM heap**.
372: 
373: - **The Problem**: In standard C/C++, constant strings like `"<!DOCTYPE html>..."` are copied from Flash ROM into SRAM upon startup. Storing 12 KB of CSS and HTML templates in SRAM would consume nearly 4% of total heap memory just holding static strings!
374: - **The Solution**: We qualify all HTML templates with the `PROGMEM` attribute:
375:   ```cpp
376:   const char NAS_PAGE_HEADER[] PROGMEM = R"rawliteral(...);
377:   ```
378:   When sending these strings over HTTP, we wrap them with `FPSTR()`:
379:   ```cpp
380:   server.sendContent(FPSTR(NAS_PAGE_HEADER));

386: ### 6.4 Streaming Multipart File Upload (`handleFileUpload`)
387: > **The Most Critical Performance Feature**: Located in [`main.cpp#L161-L186`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L161-L186).
388: 
389: When a user uploads a 5 MB file, the ESP32 cannot store the file in RAM before saving it (since total RAM is only 320 KB). Doing so would trigger an immediate kernel panic: `Out of Memory / Heap Exhaustion`.
390: 
391: Instead, we implemented a **streaming multipart chunk parser**:
392: ```cpp
393: void handleFileUpload() {
394:   HTTPUpload& upload = server.upload();
395: 
396:   if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_START) {
397:     // 1. Create file handle on SD card
398:     uploadFile = SD.open("/" + upload.filename, FILE_WRITE);
399:   } else if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_WRITE) {
400:     // 2. Stream incoming chunk (typically 1-2 KB) directly to SD SPI bus
401:     if (uploadFile) {
402:       uploadFile.write(upload.buf, upload.currentSize);
403:     }
404:   } else if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_END) {
405:     // 3. Close handle and commit FAT32 directory table
406:     if (uploadFile) {
407:       uploadFile.close();
408:     }
409:   }
410: }
411: ```
412: 
413: ```text
414: [Browser: 10MB File] 
415:        │ 
416:        ▼ (Packets in 1.4KB MTU chunks)
417: [ESP32 Network Buffer: 2KB] ──> [uploadFile.write()] ──> [MicroSD Card Blocks]
418:        │
419:    (Flushed immediately; RAM freed for next chunk)
420: ```
421: **Key Takeaway**: Regardless of whether a file is 10 KB or 100 MB, the RAM consumption remains constant at approximately 2 KB!
422: 
423: ---
424: 
425: ### 6.5 Dual-Core FreeRTOS Multitasking
426: The ESP32 features two Xtensa cores:
427: - **Core 0**: Dedicated by default to the ESP-IDF Wi-Fi/Bluetooth stack and RF modulation.
428: - **Core 1**: Executes the standard Arduino `setup()` and `loop()`.
429: 
430: In our project, we spawn an independent diagnostic thread onto Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`:
431: ```cpp
432: xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(runClientTests, "ClientTest", 6144, NULL, 1, NULL, 1);
433: ```
434: This demonstrates true preemptive multitasking on bare metal. The web server continues serving user requests in `loop()` while the diagnostic worker validates network endpoints asynchronously.
435:

442: ### 7.1 Tri-Platform Architectural Comparison Matrix
443: To understand why this project is structured into [`LocalConfig/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) and [`CloudConfig/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig), and how it transitions to physical silicon, consider this architectural matrix:
444: 
445: | Evaluation Criterion | Wokwi Web (`CloudConfig/`) | VS Code Local (`LocalConfig/`) | Physical Silicon (ESP32 DevKit V1) |
446: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
447: | **Execution Host** | Remote Cloud Containers (wokwi.com) | Local Workstation CPU via QEMU/Wasm | Physical Xtensa LX6 Dual-Core @ 240 MHz |
448: | **Subscription Cost** | Free basic; **Paid ($7-15/mo)** for inbound Private Gateway | **100% Free** (Community License) | One-time hardware (~650–900 BDT / $6–$8 USD) |
449: | **Browser GUI Access** | ❌ Inbound blocked on free tier | ✅ Full interactive (`localhost:9080`) | ✅ Full native Wi-Fi IP on Port 80 |
450: | **Live File Upload** | ❌ Blocked by cloud boundary | ✅ Full desktop drag-and-drop upload | ✅ Full upload from any phone or PC on Wi-Fi |
451: | **Storage Medium** | Ephemeral virtual RAM disk | Virtual FAT32 block storage | Physical MicroSD Card (1 GB to 32 GB) |
452: | **Persistence** | Resets on browser reload | Resets on simulation restart | **Non-volatile**: Survives complete power cutoff |
453: | **Network Autonomy** | Requires active internet connection | **100% offline** once dependencies are ready | **100% autonomous & air-gapped** (No PC needed) |

457: ### 7.2 The Wokwi Cloud Paywall & Free In-Simulation Loopback Solution
458: > **High-Yield Presentation Topic**: Demonstrates mastery of embedded network stacks and cloud container limitations.
459: 
460: When attempting to access Wokwi Web via an external browser, users encounter:
461: ```text
462: This feature is only available for paying users: https://wokwi.com/pricing
463: ```
464: - **The Technical Cause**: Wokwi's free tier provides a **Public Gateway** allowing outbound NAT (HTTP GET/POST to public APIs), but blocks inbound TCP connections from external host browsers unless subscribing to the paid "Private IoT Gateway" (\$7–\$15/mo).
465: - **The Cloud Solution ([`Project.MM/CloudConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig))**: As detailed in [`[Cloud]implementationStepsMM.PDF.pdf`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/doc/research/%5BCloud%5DimplementationStepsMM.PDF.pdf), we implement an **In-Simulation Self-Test Client (`runClientTests`)** on FreeRTOS Core 1. It queries the active `WebServer` over the internal loopback socket (`http://127.0.0.1/`), verifying status 200 responses, static site streaming, and file downloads directly in the cloud console for free!
466: - **The Local Solution ([`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig))**: By running locally in VS Code with `wokwigw.exe`, traffic stays on your machine, granting unrestricted browser access (`http://localhost:9080/`) completely for free.
467: 
468: ---
469: 
470: ### 7.3 Multi-Device LAN Accessibility (Phones & External PCs)
471: > **Evaluator Query**: *"Does this only work on localhost, or can other devices on the network connect to it?"*
472: 
473: **Answer: Any device on the same local Wi-Fi, Windows Mobile Hotspot, or wired LAN switch can simultaneously access the simulated file server!**
474: 
475: #### 1. Why Multi-Interface Routing Works (`0.0.0.0:9080` Binding)
476: - The network bridge `wokwigw.exe` binds by default to socket address `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), not just loopback `127.0.0.1`.
477: - This means it listens on **all active network interfaces** on your Windows host machine at the same time.
478: - **Firewall Rule Automation**: Windows Firewall blocks unprompted inbound connections by default. Running [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) automatically requests UAC elevation and opens TCP port 9080 across all profiles via:
479:   ```powershell
480:   New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Wokwi Gateway NAS" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 9080 -Protocol TCP -Profile Any -Action Allow
481:   ```
482: 
483: #### 2. Dual Deployment Configurations:
484: * **Method A (Wireless Hotspot)**: Turn on **Windows Mobile Hotspot** (Settings > Network & internet > Mobile hotspot). Windows assigns the host PC virtual gateway IP **`192.168.137.1`**. Evaluators connect their smartphones/tablets to this hotspot and open `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`. No campus router or Wi-Fi login is required!
485: * **Method B (Wired Ethernet LAN)**: Plug into the lab Ethernet switch. Find your host IP via `ipconfig` (e.g., `192.168.1.105`). Any lab desktop PC on the switch navigates to `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/`.
486: 
487: #### 3. Complete Host IP & Endpoint Mapping Table
488: 
489: | Network Interface | Target Client Device | Host IP Reference | NAS Explorer URL | Static Website URL |
490: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
491: | **Localhost (Loopback)** | Host workstation running VS Code | `localhost` or `127.0.0.1` | [http://localhost:9080/](http://localhost:9080/) | [http://localhost:9080/site](http://localhost:9080/site) |
492: | **Windows Mobile Hotspot** | Evaluator smartphones, tablets, laptops | `192.168.137.1` | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` | `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site` |
493: | **Wired Ethernet LAN** | Lab workstation PCs on campus network | `<YOUR_LAN_IP>` *(from `ipconfig`)* | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/` | `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/site` |
494: 
495: - **Internal Web Server**: The HTTP server is **100% native to the ESP32 C++ firmware** (`WebServer server(80)`). There is **no Apache or Nginx** running on the PC; the microcontroller itself handles socket creation, routing, and FAT32 streaming.
496: 
497: #### 7.3.1 LocalSend Web Model: 2-Computer Lab File Sharing
498: In popular file-transfer tools like **LocalSend**, the **"Share via Browser" (LocalSend Web)** feature enables zero-installation file sharing: one computer starts a temporary web server on the local network, and any other device on the LAN navigates to that IP in a browser to upload or download files without installing an app.
499: 
500: `Project.MM` reproduces this exact user-friendly workflow for laboratory evaluations, but with key **microprocessor architecture advantages**:
501: 1. **Zero Client Setup**: Neither Computer 1 nor Computer 2 needs specialized software installed. A standard browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) is all that is required.
502: 2. **True Embedded Hardware Node**: Unlike LocalSend Web (which is a heavy software desktop program running on an OS with 16 GB RAM and storing files on an internal PC SSD), `Project.MM` executes on an **ESP32 microcontroller** interfacing a **FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware VSPI bus**.
503: 3. **Decoupled Standalone Appliance**: Both computers are equal clients to the ESP32 storage pool. File exchanges do not depend on the sender's desktop OS remaining awake.
504: 4. **Strict ~2 KB Streaming Window**: File transfers never buffer entirely in memory, guaranteeing that the 520 KB SRAM limit is never breached.
505:

508: ### 7.4 Physical Bill of Materials (BOM) & Local Sourcing
509: 
510: Building the physical hardware version requires only three inexpensive, locally accessible parts:
511: 
512: | Component | Technical Model | Local Cost (BDT) | Role in System |
513: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
514: | **Microcontroller** | ESP32 DevKit V1 (30-pin, ESP-WROOM-32) | ~350–450 BDT | Core 240 MHz dual-core CPU, Wi-Fi radio, web server |
515: | **Storage Module** | MicroSD Card SPI Adapter Module | ~60–100 BDT | Physical SPI socket with level shifters & capacitors |
516: | **MicroSD Card** | Standard Class 10 MicroSD (4GB to 32GB, FAT32) | ~200–350 BDT | Physical FAT32 block storage media |
517: | **Jumper Wires** | Female-to-Female Dupont Wires (6 wires, <15cm) | ~20 BDT | High-frequency SPI interconnection |
518: | **Total Cost** | — | **~630–920 BDT ($6–$8)** | Complete autonomous, battery-powered edge NAS |

522: ### 7.5 Classic ESP32 (SPI Module) vs. ESP32-S3 (USB Host) Trade-Off
523: As evaluated in [`__which_one_would_be_better_for_the_project_.md`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/doc/research/__which_one_would_be_better_for_the_project_.md):
524: - **Why Classic ESP32 + SPI Module Wins**: Matches your submitted lab proposal pinout table (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`), costs 50% less, has rock-solid driver maturity in Arduino Core (`SD.h`), and matches the Wokwi simulation pin-for-pin.
525: - **When to Use ESP32-S3**: Only required if attaching a standard **USB thumb drive** or **USB external hard drive** directly via `usb_host_msc`.
526:

529: ### 7.6 Autonomous Off-Grid Operation: SoftAP Mode (`192.168.4.1`)
530: In real-world field deployments (or classroom demonstrations without reliable Wi-Fi), the physical ESP32 can act as its own autonomous Wi-Fi router:
531: ```cpp
532: // Change in setup():
533: WiFi.softAP("ESP32-Edge-NAS", "12345678");
534: ```
535: - The ESP32 broadcasts its own SSID: `"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`.
536: - Runs an internal DHCP server issuing IPs in the `192.168.4.x` subnet.
537: - Users connect their smartphone directly to the ESP32 Wi-Fi and open `http://192.168.4.1/`. It operates completely off-grid with zero internet, zero router, and zero PC required!

653: 
654: ## 9. Evaluator Q&A Defense (Anticipated Questions & Rebuttals)
655: 
656: ### Q1: Why ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi?
657: - **Cost**: An ESP32 is \$4, whereas a Raspberry Pi 4 is \$45 to \$75.
658: - **Power Consumption**: ESP32 consumes 80 mA to 150 mA at 3.3V (<0.5 Watt). A Raspberry Pi draws 3 to 7 Watts. An ESP32 can run for weeks on a standard 18650 lithium battery.
659: - **Boot Time**: ESP32 boots in less than 500 milliseconds. A Raspberry Pi takes 25 to 45 seconds to boot Linux.
660: - **Security**: There is no underlying Linux OS, no open SSH ports, no shell vulnerabilities, and no kernel root exploits.
661: 
662: ---
663: 
664: ### Q2: What happens if an uploaded file exceeds the ESP32 RAM?
665: - **Rebuttal**: Our upload architecture does not load the file into RAM. It uses the `server.upload()` streaming callback. Incoming TCP packets are received in small buffers (1.4 KB) and immediately flushed over SPI to the MicroSD card before the next packet arrives. As a result, the RAM usage remains static regardless of whether the file is 10 KB or 100 MB.
666: 
667: ---
668: 
669: ### Q3: Can this simulation firmware run on real, physical hardware?
670: - **Rebuttal**: **Yes, 100% without code changes.**
671:   The pins used (`GPIO 5`, `GPIO 18`, `GPIO 19`, `GPIO 23`) are the exact standard hardware VSPI pins of the ESP32 DevKit V1. If you wire a physical MicroSD breakout module to those pins and flash this firmware, the only change needed is replacing the SSID `"Wokwi-GUEST"` with your local home or university Wi-Fi network name.
672: 
673: ---
674: 
675: ### Q4: Why SPI mode for the SD card instead of 4-bit SDMMC?
676: - **Rebuttal**: While 4-bit SDMMC offers higher bandwidth, it requires 6 specific dedicated pins (including GPIO 12, which is an internal strapping pin that can brick bootup if pulled high at power-on). SPI mode requires only 4 pins, has universal compatibility across all SD and MicroSD breakout boards, and provides plenty of bandwidth for low-power edge NAS operations.
677: 
678: ---
679: 
680: ### Q5: How does the web server avoid blocking other background tasks?
681: - **Rebuttal**: We take advantage of the ESP32's dual-core Xtensa architecture and the FreeRTOS real-time operating system. Time-critical background operations (like sensor telemetry or network health tests) are pinned to Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`, while the networking stack runs independently on Core 0.
682: 
683: ---
684: 
685: ### Q6: Does the file server only work on localhost, or can other network devices connect?
686: - **Rebuttal**: It is fully accessible across the local network. In our simulation, `wokwigw.exe` binds to `0.0.0.0:9080`, allowing any smartphone or PC on the same Wi-Fi to access the NAS at `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/`. On physical hardware, the ESP32 connects directly to the Wi-Fi router (or broadcasts its own SoftAP), serving all network devices natively on standard port 80 with no host PC required.
687: 
688: ---
689: 
690: ### Q7: Why did Wokwi Cloud show a paywall, and how does your project bypass it?
691: - **Rebuttal**: Wokwi Cloud's free tier provides a Public Gateway that only supports outbound NAT requests (e.g. hitting weather APIs), but blocks inbound TCP connections from external desktop browsers unless subscribing to their paid Private Gateway ($7–$15/mo). We bypassed this in two ways:
692:   1. For cloud users, [`Project.MM/CloudConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig) uses an internal FreeRTOS loopback client (`runClientTests` on `127.0.0.1`) that tests all endpoints 100% for free inside the simulator.
693:   2. For full interactive browser testing, [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) runs locally in VS Code with the free community license and local `wokwigw.exe` bridge.
694: 
695: ---
696: 
697: ### Q8: Why choose Classic ESP32 with SPI over an ESP32-S3 with a USB flash drive?
698: - **Rebuttal**: The Classic ESP32 (WROOM-32) with a SPI MicroSD module costs under 400 BDT, is ubiquitously available, has a mature, rock-solid Arduino `SD` library, and aligns 100% with the pinout table submitted in our course proposal (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`). While the ESP32-S3 supports native USB host for pen drives, it requires complex USB MSC drivers and different pin configurations.
699: 
700: ---
701: 
702: ### Q9: How would this system operate in a field environment without an internet router?
703: - **Rebuttal**: The ESP32 natively supports **Soft Access Point (SoftAP) Mode** (`WiFi.softAP()`). In an off-grid forest or disaster zone, the ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID (`"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`). Field personnel connect their smartphones directly to the ESP32 and access files at `http://192.168.4.1/` without needing an internet connection, external router, or PC.
704: 
705: ---
706: 
707: ### Q10: How does this system compare to LocalSend / LocalSend Web?
708: - **Rebuttal**: LocalSend's "Share via Browser" (Web Share) mode turns a desktop PC into a temporary web server on the local network so other machines can transfer files in a browser without installing the app. Our project provides that exact same zero-install browser experience for lab computers. However, from an embedded systems perspective, `Project.MM` is fundamentally distinct: it runs on a \$4 ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB SRAM rather than a multi-gigabyte PC OS, writes files across hardware VSPI lines directly into FAT32 MicroSD card sectors with a strict ~2 KB RAM streaming overhead, and acts as an autonomous hardware appliance that does not depend on a host PC remaining online.
709: 
710: ---
711: 
712: ### Q11: How do you handle campus Wi-Fi AP/Client Isolation during a lab demonstration?
713: - **Rebuttal**: University routers and enterprise switches often enforce AP/Client Isolation to prevent peer-to-peer communication between connected devices. To guarantee that our live demonstration is never blocked by institutional firewall policies, we activate **Windows Mobile Hotspot** on the host workstation. Windows configures a virtual NAT gateway at `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or lab computer connecting to this hotspot can reach `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router restrictions.
714: 
715: ---

20: ## Overview
21: This project sets up, compiles, simulates, and serves an ESP32-based Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server entirely on your local workstation using the **Wokwi for VS Code** extension and **PlatformIO IDE**.
22: 
23: By running simulation locally, the ESP32 code executes via your local compiler toolchain without cloud rate limits, and network requests can be bridged directly to your host PC loopback adapter (`localhost:9080`) as well as external network interfaces (wired Ethernet and wireless Mobile Hotspot).

139: ### 2.2 The Standalone Workspace Philosophy
140: One of the most critical structural decisions made in this repository is **workspace decoupling**:
141: - All installation scripts and dependency managers live in [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup).
142: - The active simulation project [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) is completely self-contained. It contains its own `wokwigw.exe`, `diagram.json`, and `wokwi.toml`.
143: - **Why this matters for your presentation**: If an evaluator asks you to clone the repo or open the project on another laptop, you do **not** have to run everything from the root. You simply open `LocalConfig` in VS Code, start the gateway, press `F1`, and run.

85: ### 1.2 Project Scope & Real-World Goals
86: 1. **Air-Gapped Field Data Logging**: In remote industrial sites, environmental sensors can log high-frequency telemetry onto an SD card; field engineers can walk up, connect via local Wi-Fi, and download data or manage logs through an intuitive web UI without any internet connection.
87: 2. **Decentralized Emergency Web Node**: In disaster-relief zones or off-grid scenarios, this node can broadcast emergency static documentation, evacuation maps, and survival guides stored directly on physical flash media.
88: 3. **Ultra-Low Cost & Zero Maintenance**: No spinning hard drives, no noisy fans, zero Linux OS kernel overhead, and instant boot times (< 1 second) with zero vulnerability to common operating system zero-day exploits.
89: 
90: ### 1.3 Core Technical Highlights
91: | Dimension | Specification |
92: | :--- | :--- |
93: | **Microcontroller** | ESP32-WROOM-32 (Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 @ 240 MHz) |
94: | **Volatile RAM** | 520 KB Internal SRAM (320 KB accessible to user heap) |
95: | **Firmware Flash** | 4 MB SPI Flash (Stores compiled code & UI templates via `PROGMEM`) |
96: | **Peripheral Storage** | Virtual MicroSD Block Device formatted with FAT32 |
97: | **Hardware Bus** | VSPI Hardware Peripheral (GPIO 18, 19, 23, 5) |
98: | **Networking** | 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi + HTTP/1.1 REST Web Server |
99: | **Concurrency** | FreeRTOS Multitasking (Core 0 network stack, Core 1 web server & diagnostics) |
100: | **UI Aesthetics** | Glassmorphic Dark UI (`Inter` typography, CSS3 gradients, storage progress bar) |

148: ### 2.2 The Standalone Workspace Philosophy
149: One of the most critical structural decisions made in this repository is **workspace decoupling**:
150: - All installation scripts and dependency managers live in [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup/`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup).

152: - **Why this matters for your presentation**: If an evaluator asks you to clone the repo or open the project on another laptop, you do **not** have to run everything from the root. You simply open `LocalConfig` in VS Code, start the gateway, press `F1`, and run.

215: ### 3.3 Clock Pin Identifier Nuance (`SCK` vs `CLK`)
216: On standard SPI breakout boards, the clock pin is often labeled `CLK`. In Wokwi's internal part manifest for `wokwi-microsd-card`, the pin is strictly named `SCK`. Using `sd1:CLK` fails schema validation. We corrected this to `sd1:SCK`, ensuring a clean physical layer simulation.

220: ## 4. Environment Setup & Toolchain Pipeline
221: 
222: ### 4.1 Compilation Pipeline: From C++ to Flash Binary
223: Embedded development differs fundamentally from interpreted languages (Python/JS). Here is how our code transitions from source to execution:
224: 
225: ```mermaid
226: flowchart LR
227:     A[main.cpp] --> C[PlatformIO Compiler / xtensa-esp32-elf-g++]
228:     B[html_templates.h] --> C
229:     D[Arduino Core / SPI / SD / WebServer] --> C
230:     C --> E[Linker: firmware.elf]
231:     E --> F[ESP-IDF esptool.py]
232:     F --> G[firmware.bin 1.24 MB]
233:     G --> H[Wokwi Virtual Flash]
234: ```
235: 
236: 1. **Preprocessing & Inclusion**: `#include "html_templates.h"` in [`main.cpp`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp) injects the HTML layout structures into the translation unit.
237: 2. **Xtensa Cross-Compilation**: `xtensa-esp32-elf-g++` compiles C++ code into machine instructions for the 32-bit Xtensa LX6 architecture.
238: 3. **Firmware Packaging**: PlatformIO invokes `esptool.py` to merge code, bootloader, and partition tables into `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin` (approx. 1.24 MB).
239: 4. **Wokwi Loading**: [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) points directly to this `.bin` file, loading it into virtual SPI flash at address `0x10000`.
240: 
241: ---
242: 
243: ### 4.2 Networking Bridge Architecture (Wokwi Gateway)
244: By default, the Wokwi simulator runs inside an isolated web sandboxed container. The simulated ESP32 connects to an emulated Wi-Fi network (`Wokwi-GUEST`) and is assigned a private IP address (`10.13.37.2`).
245: 
246: Because `10.13.37.2` exists only within the simulator, your host computer's browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) cannot reach it directly. To bridge this gap, we use the **Wokwi IoT Gateway (`wokwigw`)**:
247: 
248: ```mermaid
249: flowchart TD
250:     subgraph Host Computer
251:         Browser[Web Browser: Chrome/Firefox]
252:         GW[Wokwi IoT Gateway: wokwigw.exe]
253:         VSC[VS Code Wokwi Simulator]
254:     end
255: 
256:     subgraph Emulated Network
257:         ESP[Simulated ESP32 NAS Node]
258:     end
259: 
260:     Browser -- "HTTP GET / POST (localhost:9080)" --> GW
261:     GW -- "Port Forward (9080 -> 10.13.37.2:80)" --> GW
262:     GW -- "WebSocket Bridge (ws://localhost:9011)" --> VSC
263:     VSC -- "Virtual Ethernet Frames" --> ESP
264:     ESP -- "HTTP 200 / Streamed Data" --> VSC
265:     VSC -- "WebSocket" --> GW
266:     GW -- "HTTP Response" --> Browser
267: ```
268: 
269: 1. [`wokwi.toml`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/wokwi.toml) specifies `[net] gateway = "ws://localhost:9011"`.
270: 2. Running `.\wokwigw.exe --forward 9080:10.13.37.2:80` opens a WebSocket server on port `9011` and an HTTP listener on port `9080`.
271: 3. When you open `http://localhost:9080/`, the gateway translates standard TCP packets into Wokwi Ethernet packets, routing them straight to the virtual ESP32.
272:

340: ### 5.2 Phase 1: Storage Subsystem & Directory Seeding
341: Located in [`main.cpp#L29-L91`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L29-L91):
342: 1. **Explicit VSPI Bus Binding**:
343:    ```cpp
344:    SPI.begin(18, 19, 23, SD_CS_PIN);
345:    SD.begin(SD_CS_PIN, SPI);
346:    ```
347:    Unlike Arduino Uno which only has one SPI bus, the ESP32 has multiple multiplexed buses. Explicitly binding pins prevents pin collision.
348: 2. **Capacity Diagnostics**: Calculates total capacity and used space via `SD.totalBytes()` and `SD.usedBytes()`.
349: 3. **Dynamic Block Device Seeding**:
350:    If the SD card has never been formatted or is blank:
351:    - Creates the directory `/www` via `SD.mkdir("/www")`.
352:    - Writes the static website [`SEED_INDEX_HTML`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h#L264-L387) into `/www/index.html`.
353:    - Creates a default metadata file `/lab_report.txt`.
354: 4. **Directory Traversal**: Recursively scans `/` using `root.openNextFile()` and prints the file tree to the Serial Monitor.
355: 
356: ---
357: 
358: ### 5.3 Phase 2: Network Subsystem, REST Routing & FreeRTOS Telemetry
359: Located in [`main.cpp#L93-L305`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L93-L305):
360: 1. **Virtual Wi-Fi Initialization**: Connects to `Wokwi-GUEST` with non-blocking status polling.
361: 2. **RESTful HTTP Endpoint Table**:
362: 
363: | Method | Endpoint | Handler | Action Performed |
364: | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
365: | `GET` | `/` | `handleRoot` | Dynamically builds storage meter, upload form, and file list |
366: | `GET` | `/site` | `handleSite` | Streams `/www/index.html` from SD card with `text/html` MIME |
367: | `GET` | `/get?file=<name>` | `handleDownload` | Streams file binary with `application/octet-stream` header |
368: | `POST`| `/upload` | `handleFileUpload` | Parses incoming multipart stream and writes blocks to SD |
369: | `GET` | `/delete?file=<n>` | `handleDelete` | Deletes file from SD via `SD.remove()` and redirects to `/` |
370: 
371: 3. **Background Diagnostic Task (`runClientTests`)**:
372:    - Uses FreeRTOS `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore` with a 6144-byte stack on Core 1.
373:    - Waits 4 seconds after boot, then executes HTTP client requests against `http://127.0.0.1/` to verify that all endpoints return HTTP `200 OK`.
374:    - Automatically deallocates itself using `vTaskDelete(NULL)`.

380: ### 6.1 Modular HTML Architecture (`include/html_templates.h`)
381: In novice embedded projects, developers often embed HTML directly inside C++ functions as long, messy string concatenations (`String html = "<html>..."; html += "<body>...";`). This leads to unmaintainable code and rapid heap fragmentation.
382: 
383: We resolved this by isolating the entire presentation layer into [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h):
384: - **C++ Raw String Literals**:
385:   ```cpp
386:   const char NAS_PAGE_HEADER[] PROGMEM = R"rawliteral(
387:   <!DOCTYPE html>
388:   <html>
389:   ...
390:   </html>

391: ### 6.1 Modular HTML Architecture (`include/html_templates.h`)
392: In novice embedded projects, developers often embed HTML directly inside C++ functions as long, messy string concatenations (`String html = "<html>..."; html += "<body>...";`). This leads to unmaintainable code and rapid heap fragmentation.
393: 
394: We resolved this by isolating the entire presentation layer into [`Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/include/html_templates.h):
395: - **C++ Raw String Literals**:
396:   ```cpp
397:   const char NAS_PAGE_HEADER[] PROGMEM = R"rawliteral(
398:   <!DOCTYPE html>
399:   <html>
400:   ...
401:   </html>
402:   )rawliteral";
403:   ```
404:   Using `R"rawliteral(...)rawliteral"` eliminates the need to escape quotes (`\"`) or newlines (`\n`), allowing clean HTML/CSS to be authored exactly as it would appear in a web editor.
405: 
406: ---
407: 
408: ### 6.2 Dispelling the "Single File Flashing" Embedded Myth
409: > **Anticipated Evaluator Question**: *"Since the ESP32 is a microchip, don't we have to write all our code in a single file so it can be flashed?"*
410: 
411: **The Answer**: **No. That is a common misunderstanding of how embedded toolchains operate.**
412: 
413: 1. **Software Engineering Phase (PC Side)**: You can split your code into dozens of `.h` header files and `.cpp` implementation files. This maintains modularity, readability, and separation of concerns.
414: 2. **Compilation & Linking Phase**: The C++ compiler (`xtensa-esp32-elf-g++`) compiles each `.cpp` into an object file (`.o`). The linker then links all object files, libraries (`SD`, `SPI`, `WiFi`), and templates into a single unified binary file: `.pio/build/esp32dev/firmware.bin`.
415: 3. **Flashing Phase (Hardware Side)**: The physical flasher (`esptool.py`) writes that single `.bin` file into the ESP32's flash memory.
416: 
417: Therefore, modularizing HTML into `include/html_templates.h` has **zero** runtime penalty and represents industry-standard embedded software engineering.
418: 
419: ---
420: 
421: ### 6.3 Flash Memory Management via `PROGMEM` and `FPSTR`
422: The ESP32 has **4 MB of external SPI Flash ROM**, but only **320 KB of usable internal SRAM heap**.
423: 
424: - **The Problem**: In standard C/C++, constant strings like `"<!DOCTYPE html>..."` are copied from Flash ROM into SRAM upon startup. Storing 12 KB of CSS and HTML templates in SRAM would consume nearly 4% of total heap memory just holding static strings!
425: - **The Solution**: We qualify all HTML templates with the `PROGMEM` attribute:
426:   ```cpp
427:   const char NAS_PAGE_HEADER[] PROGMEM = R"rawliteral(...);
428:   ```
429:   When sending these strings over HTTP, we wrap them with `FPSTR()`:
430:   ```cpp
431:   server.sendContent(FPSTR(NAS_PAGE_HEADER));
432:   ```
433:   `FPSTR` instructs the web server to read bytes directly out of Flash ROM memory space, leaving the 320 KB SRAM completely free for network buffers and filesystem I/O.
434: 
435: ---
436: 
437: ### 6.4 Streaming Multipart File Upload (`handleFileUpload`)
438: > **The Most Critical Performance Feature**: Located in [`main.cpp#L161-L186`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp#L161-L186).
439: 
440: When a user uploads a 5 MB file, the ESP32 cannot store the file in RAM before saving it (since total RAM is only 320 KB). Doing so would trigger an immediate kernel panic: `Out of Memory / Heap Exhaustion`.
441: 
442: Instead, we implemented a **streaming multipart chunk parser**:
443: ```cpp
444: void handleFileUpload() {
445:   HTTPUpload& upload = server.upload();
446: 
447:   if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_START) {
448:     // 1. Create file handle on SD card
449:     uploadFile = SD.open("/" + upload.filename, FILE_WRITE);
450:   } else if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_WRITE) {
451:     // 2. Stream incoming chunk (typically 1-2 KB) directly to SD SPI bus
452:     if (uploadFile) {
453:       uploadFile.write(upload.buf, upload.currentSize);
454:     }
455:   } else if (upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_END) {
456:     // 3. Close handle and commit FAT32 directory table
457:     if (uploadFile) {
458:       uploadFile.close();
459:     }
460:   }
461: }
462: ```
463: 
464: ```text
465: [Browser: 10MB File] 
466:        │ 
467:        ▼ (Packets in 1.4KB MTU chunks)
468: [ESP32 Network Buffer: 2KB] ──> [uploadFile.write()] ──> [MicroSD Card Blocks]
469:        │
470:    (Flushed immediately; RAM freed for next chunk)
471: ```
472: **Key Takeaway**: Regardless of whether a file is 10 KB or 100 MB, the RAM consumption remains constant at approximately 2 KB!
473: 
474: ---
475: 
476: ### 6.5 Dual-Core FreeRTOS Multitasking
477: The ESP32 features two Xtensa cores:
478: - **Core 0**: Dedicated by default to the ESP-IDF Wi-Fi/Bluetooth stack and RF modulation.
479: - **Core 1**: Executes the standard Arduino `setup()` and `loop()`.
480: 
481: In our project, we spawn an independent diagnostic thread onto Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`:
482: ```cpp
483: xTaskCreatePinnedToCore(runClientTests, "ClientTest", 6144, NULL, 1, NULL, 1);
484: ```
485: This demonstrates true preemptive multitasking on bare metal. The web server continues serving user requests in `loop()` while the diagnostic worker validates network endpoints asynchronously.
486: 
487: ---
488:

584: ### 7.5 Classic ESP32 (SPI Module) vs. ESP32-S3 (USB Host) Trade-Off
585: As evaluated in [`__which_one_would_be_better_for_the_project_.md`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/doc/research/__which_one_would_be_better_for_the_project_.md):
586: - **Why Classic ESP32 + SPI Module Wins**: Matches your submitted lab proposal pinout table (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`), costs 50% less, has rock-solid driver maturity in Arduino Core (`SD.h`), and matches the Wokwi simulation pin-for-pin.
587: - **When to Use ESP32-S3**: Only required if attaching a standard **USB thumb drive** or **USB external hard drive** directly via `usb_host_msc`.
588: 
589: ---
590: 
591: ### 7.6 Autonomous Off-Grid Operation: SoftAP Mode (`192.168.4.1`)
592: In real-world field deployments (or classroom demonstrations without reliable Wi-Fi), the physical ESP32 can act as its own autonomous Wi-Fi router:
593: ```cpp
594: // Change in setup():
595: WiFi.softAP("ESP32-Edge-NAS", "12345678");
596: ```
597: - The ESP32 broadcasts its own SSID: `"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`.
598: - Runs an internal DHCP server issuing IPs in the `192.168.4.x` subnet.
599: - Users connect their smartphone directly to the ESP32 Wi-Fi and open `http://192.168.4.1/`. It operates completely off-grid with zero internet, zero router, and zero PC required!

716: ## 9. Evaluator Q&A Defense (Anticipated Questions & Rebuttals)
717: 
718: ### Q1: Why ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi?
719: - **Cost**: An ESP32 is \$4, whereas a Raspberry Pi 4 is \$45 to \$75.
720: - **Power Consumption**: ESP32 consumes 80 mA to 150 mA at 3.3V (<0.5 Watt). A Raspberry Pi draws 3 to 7 Watts. An ESP32 can run for weeks on a standard 18650 lithium battery.
721: - **Boot Time**: ESP32 boots in less than 500 milliseconds. A Raspberry Pi takes 25 to 45 seconds to boot Linux.
722: - **Security**: There is no underlying Linux OS, no open SSH ports, no shell vulnerabilities, and no kernel root exploits.
723: 
724: ---
725: 
726: ### Q2: What happens if an uploaded file exceeds the ESP32 RAM?
727: - **Rebuttal**: Our upload architecture does not load the file into RAM. It uses the `server.upload()` streaming callback. Incoming TCP packets are received in small buffers (1.4 KB) and immediately flushed over SPI to the MicroSD card before the next packet arrives. As a result, the RAM usage remains static regardless of whether the file is 10 KB or 100 MB.
728: 
729: ---
730: 
731: ### Q3: Can this simulation firmware run on real, physical hardware?
732: - **Rebuttal**: **Yes, 100% without code changes.**
733:   The pins used (`GPIO 5`, `GPIO 18`, `GPIO 19`, `GPIO 23`) are the exact standard hardware VSPI pins of the ESP32 DevKit V1. If you wire a physical MicroSD breakout module to those pins and flash this firmware, the only change needed is replacing the SSID `"Wokwi-GUEST"` with your local home or university Wi-Fi network name.
734: 
735: ---
736: 
737: ### Q4: Why SPI mode for the SD card instead of 4-bit SDMMC?
738: - **Rebuttal**: While 4-bit SDMMC offers higher bandwidth, it requires 6 specific dedicated pins (including GPIO 12, which is an internal strapping pin that can brick bootup if pulled high at power-on). SPI mode requires only 4 pins, has universal compatibility across all SD and MicroSD breakout boards, and provides plenty of bandwidth for low-power edge NAS operations.
739: 
740: ---
741: 
742: ### Q5: How does the web server avoid blocking other background tasks?
743: - **Rebuttal**: We take advantage of the ESP32's dual-core Xtensa architecture and the FreeRTOS real-time operating system. Time-critical background operations (like sensor telemetry or network health tests) are pinned to Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`, while the networking stack runs independently on Core 0.
744: 
745: ---
746: 
747: ### Q6: Does the file server only work on localhost, or can other network devices connect?
748: - **Rebuttal**: It is fully accessible across the local network. In our simulation, `wokwigw.exe` binds to `0.0.0.0:9080`, allowing any smartphone or PC on the same Wi-Fi to access the NAS at `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/`. On physical hardware, the ESP32 connects directly to the Wi-Fi router (or broadcasts its own SoftAP), serving all network devices natively on standard port 80 with no host PC required.
749: 
750: ---
751: 
752: ### Q7: Why did Wokwi Cloud show a paywall, and how does your project bypass it?
753: - **Rebuttal**: Wokwi Cloud's free tier provides a Public Gateway that only supports outbound NAT requests (e.g. hitting weather APIs), but blocks inbound TCP connections from external desktop browsers unless subscribing to their paid Private Gateway ($7–$15/mo). We bypassed this in two ways:
754:   1. For cloud users, [`Project.MM/CloudConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig) uses an internal FreeRTOS loopback client (`runClientTests` on `127.0.0.1`) that tests all endpoints 100% for free inside the simulator.
755:   2. For full interactive browser testing, [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) runs locally in VS Code with the free community license and local `wokwigw.exe` bridge.
756: 
757: ---
758: 
759: ### Q8: Why choose Classic ESP32 with SPI over an ESP32-S3 with a USB flash drive?
760: - **Rebuttal**: The Classic ESP32 (WROOM-32) with a SPI MicroSD module costs under 400 BDT, is ubiquitously available, has a mature, rock-solid Arduino `SD` library, and aligns 100% with the pinout table submitted in our course proposal (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`). While the ESP32-S3 supports native USB host for pen drives, it requires complex USB MSC drivers and different pin configurations.
761: 
762: ---
763: 
764: ### Q9: How would this system operate in a field environment without an internet router?
765: - **Rebuttal**: The ESP32 natively supports **Soft Access Point (SoftAP) Mode** (`WiFi.softAP()`). In an off-grid forest or disaster zone, the ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID (`"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`). Field personnel connect their smartphones directly to the ESP32 and access files at `http://192.168.4.1/` without needing an internet connection, external router, or PC.
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ### Q10: How does this system compare to LocalSend / LocalSend Web?
770: - **Rebuttal**: LocalSend's "Share via Browser" (Web Share) mode turns a desktop PC into a temporary web server on the local network so other machines can transfer files in a browser without installing the app. Our project provides that exact same zero-install browser experience for lab computers. However, from an embedded systems perspective, `Project.MM` is fundamentally distinct: it runs on a \$4 ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB SRAM rather than a multi-gigabyte PC OS, writes files across hardware VSPI lines directly into FAT32 MicroSD card sectors with a strict ~2 KB RAM streaming overhead, and acts as an autonomous hardware appliance that does not depend on a host PC remaining online.
771: 
772: ---
773: 
774: ### Q11: How do you handle campus Wi-Fi AP/Client Isolation during a lab demonstration?
775: - **Rebuttal**: University routers and enterprise switches often enforce AP/Client Isolation to prevent peer-to-peer communication between connected devices. To guarantee that our live demonstration is never blocked by institutional firewall policies, we activate **Windows Mobile Hotspot** on the host workstation. Windows configures a virtual NAT gateway at `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or lab computer connecting to this hotspot can reach `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router restrictions.
776:

802: ### Q13: Why did uploads stay stuck at 100% for several seconds before completing?
803: - **Rebuttal**: In our simulation architecture, client uploads traverse the host machine's loopback interface at gigabit speed, filling the OS socket buffer almost immediately so `xhr.upload.onprogress` reaches 100% in milliseconds. However, the virtual ESP32 runs at cycle-accurate simulation speed, bit-banging and clocking each 512-byte sector across the simulated VSPI bus into the virtual FAT32 SD card. In the web UI, we introduced a dedicated commit transition state (`Writing to Storage`, `⚡ Committing...`, `⏱ Finalizing SD card write`) to explicitly inform users that network delivery has finished and the simulated microcontroller is actively committing blocks to storage.
804: 
805: ---
806: 
807: ### Q14: How does your firmware guarantee zero corrupted or 0-byte files if an upload is interrupted?
808: - **Rebuttal**: In `handleFileUpload()`, on `UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED` or on write error detection, the firmware immediately closes the active file handle and invokes `SD.remove(currentUploadTarget)`. Furthermore, the POST completion callback strictly verifies `upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_END && upload.totalSize > 0 && !uploadWriteError`; otherwise, it returns HTTP 500 JSON error. This ensures aborted uploads never linger as empty 0-byte entries on FAT32.
809: 
810: ---
811: 
812: ### Q15: Why is the SPI clock initialized to 4 MHz rather than 25 MHz or 40 MHz?
813: - **Rebuttal**: Virtual SD card simulation in Wokwi (as well as physical Dupont jumper wires on breadboards) suffers from timing signal degradation when clocking bulk data block writes (`CMD24`/`CMD25`) above 10 MHz, causing `FR_DISK_ERR` and stream write failures. Standard 4 MHz SPI provides 100% block write reliability without clock jitter in both virtual simulation and physical hardware prototyping.
814: 
815: ---
816: 
817: ### Q16: How does the asset generation pipeline allow web developers to modify HTML without editing C++ code?
818: - **Rebuttal**: Frontend files exist as standard HTML/CSS/JS in `Project.MM/LocalConfig/data/www/` (`fileserver.html`, `index.html`), which can be edited and previewed directly in web browsers. Our build script [`refresh_firmware.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/refresh_firmware.ps1) (and its companion `refresh_firmware.bat`) automatically runs `scripts/generate_assets.ps1` to convert all web assets into PROGMEM byte arrays in `include/default_assets.h` before invoking PlatformIO. Developers never need to manually escape HTML strings inside C++ files.

80: ## 1. Executive Pitch & Project Scope
81: 
82: ### 1.1 The 30-Second Elevator Pitch
83: > *"Traditional Network Attached Storage (NAS) units and web servers rely on power-hungry single-board computers (like Raspberry Pi) or x86 servers drawing 15 to 60 Watts. In this project, we prove that an ultra-low-cost ($4), low-power (<1 Watt) ESP32 dual-core microcontroller can autonomously act as an air-gapped, zero-trust edge NAS and static web host. Interfacing a FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware SPI bus, our firmware delivers full multipart file uploads, chunked downloads, dynamic file deletion, real-time storage telemetry, and static HTML5 website hosting directly to desktop browsers via a local network bridge."*
